ai.definition: Wave energy refers to the technology that converts the kinetic and potential energy from ocean waves into electrical power. This renewable resource is harnessed using various devices designed to capture the up-and-down (heave) and side-to-side (surge) motions of waves.
ai.howItWorks: Devices such as point absorbers, oscillating water columns, or attenuators are deployed in coastal waters. These devices convert the wave motion into mechanical energy through hydraulic or direct-drive generators, which is then transformed into electrical power via a generator connected to the grid.
ai.problemSolved: Wave energy addresses the need for sustainable and reliable renewable energy sources that can complement existing grid systems, particularly in coastal regions where wave activity is high.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves designing, testing, and producing wave energy devices. This process requires specialized knowledge in marine engineering, materials science, and electrical engineering to ensure robustness against harsh ocean conditions.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes site selection, device fabrication, deployment, and integration with the existing power grid. Devices are typically anchored to the seabed or float on the surface, requiring careful placement to optimize energy capture while minimizing environmental impact.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include initial capital investment for device development and installation, ongoing maintenance costs, and the variability of wave conditions which can affect energy output predictability.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Wave energy is expected to become more commercially viable as technology matures and economies of scale are achieved. However, it still faces challenges related to environmental impact and grid integration.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks vary by region but generally require environmental assessments and adherence to safety standards for marine installations. International bodies like the International Energy Agency (IEA) provide guidelines for wave energy development.
ai.risks: Environmental risks include potential impacts on marine ecosystems, while technical risks involve device reliability in harsh ocean conditions and the variability of wave energy output.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently limited due to high initial costs and variable energy production. However, as technology improves and deployment scales, profitability may increase.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development focuses on improving efficiency, reducing environmental impact, and integrating wave energy with other renewable sources for a more robust energy mix.

glossary.def: A type of wave energy converter that captures the motion at a single point in the water column.
A device where waves push air into a chamber, driving a turbine to generate electricity.
A long, parallel array of structures that interact with the wave motion to extract energy.

subsystems.name: Wave energy converter (WEC)
subsystems.role: the moving body that captures wave motion and turns it into mechanical work or pressurised fluid.

subsystems.name: Power take-off (PTO)
subsystems.role: converts the captured motion into electricity.

subsystems.name: Mooring and foundation
subsystems.role: holds the device in place and provides a reaction point.
parts: chain, wire or synthetic mooring lines

subsystems.name: Electrical collection and export
subsystems.role: gathers power from each device and brings it ashore.

subsystems.name: Control and monitoring
subsystems.role: tunes the device to the sea state and protects it from damaging loads.

subsystems.name: Survivability systems
subsystems.role: lets the device survive storms that would otherwise destroy it.

buildSteps.title: Design and numerical modelling
buildSteps.detail: Engineers simulate wave-structure interaction and estimate power output for a chosen site's wave climate.

buildSteps.title: Scale-model testing
buildSteps.detail: Small models are tested in wave tanks and towing tanks to validate motion, mooring loads and PTO behaviour.

buildSteps.title: Component fabrication
buildSteps.detail: Steel or concrete hulls, hydraulic systems and generators are built in shipyards or fabrication yards, with marine-grade coatings.

buildSteps.title: Onshore assembly and testing
buildSteps.detail: The device is assembled and its PTO, control system and electrical equipment are run on land before going to sea.

buildSteps.title: Mooring and foundation installation
buildSteps.detail: Anchors are placed on the seabed and mooring lines are pre-laid using offshore vessels.

buildSteps.title: Offshore deployment and connection
buildSteps.detail: The device is towed to site, hooked up to its moorings, and its subsea cable is connected to the export line.

buildSteps.title: Commissioning
buildSteps.detail: Communication, control, storm mode and power export are tested under real sea conditions.

buildSteps.title: Operation and maintenance
buildSteps.detail: Remote monitoring is combined with periodic inspection and maintenance visits for the life of the device.

prerequisites.why: installing, mooring and maintaining devices at sea uses skills and vessels already common in offshore oil and wind.
hydraulic and direct-drive systems work in prototypes, but efficiency and long-term reliability need improvement.
many early devices were damaged or destroyed by storms; designs now include submergence or storm-mode survival.

prerequisites.tech: Subsea power cables and grid connection
prerequisites.why: offshore wind has already developed the cables, connectors and converters needed to bring power ashore.
steels, composites and concrete coatings are available for decades of salt-water exposure.

pathway.milestone: single-device prototypes tested at open-sea test centres, with some grid-connected
pathway.unlocks: real-world data on power output, loads and maintenance needs.

pathway.milestone: small arrays of a few devices sharing a cable and mooring area
pathway.unlocks: demonstration of reliability and operating costs at array scale.

pathway.milestone: multi-device farms co-located with offshore wind, sharing substations and vessels
pathway.unlocks: lower cost per unit through shared infrastructure and smoother combined output.

pathway.milestone: large-scale wave farms contributing steady power to coastal grids
pathway.unlocks: a predictable renewable source that complements wind and solar.
